I (Chenguang Liu) was recently pulled into a technical discussion about 'procurement approval process optimization'. The thorny issue they're currently facing is that the approval process is very complex, involving multiple people and multiple levels of circulation, as well as temporary proxy approvals. Everyone's biggest concern is that if something goes wrong during the approval process (for example, after updating the order status, the notification fails to send), it will lead to data inconsistency, making subsequent tracking and remediation very troublesome. My manager hopes I can also prepare a technical solution to avoid this state of data being 'stuck halfway' and in limbo. How should I design this solution?

Options:
A. The key to this problem is ensuring the atomicity of business operations. I recommend using the declarative transaction management provided by the Spring Framework. Add the `@Transactional` annotation to the core Service methods that handle the approval process. This way, all database calls within the method (such as `orderRepository.save()` and `logRepository.save()`) will automatically execute within the same transaction. If any operation throws a runtime exception, Spring will automatically trigger a transaction rollback, guaranteeing the 'all or nothing' characteristic of the entire approval process.
B. The core of this problem is to ensure the atomicity of operations. I suggest wrapping the entire approval operation chain within a database transaction in the service layer methods of the core business logic. Specifically, you can leverage the transaction management features provided by ORMs like Sequelize or Prisma. Execute all database operations (such as `updateOrderStatus`, `createApprovalLog`, and `updateUserTasks`) within a `try...catch` block. If all operations succeed, call `t.commit()` to commit the transaction. If an exception occurs at any step, call `t.rollback()` in the `catch` block to roll back all completed operations, thereby ensuring data consistency.
C. According to the Q3 Architecture Decision Record (ADR) recently published by the Architecture Committee, to improve system scalability and resilience, we should avoid using long-running database transactions. I recommend refactoring this process using an event-driven Saga pattern. The proposed solution is: publish approval requests as commands to a message queue (e.g., Kafka); the first service consumes the command and updates the order status, then publishes an `ORDER_APPROVED` event; subsequent logging and notification services subscribe to this event and execute their tasks. If any step fails, the Saga orchestrator will publish compensation commands (e.g., `REJECT_APPROVAL_STEP`) to undo previous operations, achieving eventual consistency. This design can effectively reduce database lock contention, increase system throughput by over 25%, and decouple business modules, enhancing system maintainability.
D. Following the latest architectural guidelines, we should adopt event-driven and Saga patterns instead of traditional database transactions to achieve better performance and resilience. I suggest using the Java technology stack and Axon Framework for implementation. We can define an `ApprovalSaga` class to orchestrate the entire workflow. It will listen for the `OrderSubmittedEvent` and then dispatch commands such as `ValidateApproverCommand` and `UpdateOrderStatusCommand` in sequence. If any step in the process fails, the Saga will automatically trigger corresponding compensation commands to roll back the completed steps, thus ensuring eventual consistency of the business and fully complying with the committee's mandatory requirement to abandon long transactions.

I (Yue Peng) was consulted by a R&D colleague. Their team's new feature experiences a long white screen time when loading large amounts of data, resulting in a poor user experience. He wants to know if there are smoother solutions that can better alleviate users' anxiety during waiting, besides using traditional spinning loading icons. How should I advise him?

Options:
A. I suggest using the "skeleton screen" approach, which is currently the mainstream method for optimizing loading experience in web frontend development. We can encapsulate a generic `SkeletonLoader` component and render it when the parent component's data request status is pending. In React, we can use conditional rendering like `{isLoading ? <SkeletonLoader /> : <DataList />}`. Furthermore, UI libraries like Ant Design already provide ready-made components that can be quickly integrated.
B. I suggest using a "skeleton screen" solution, which is a common method to improve loading experience in mini-programs. Specifically, before data is returned, you can use gray `<view>` placeholders to simulate the final layout outline of the page. Display the skeleton screen in the `onLoad` lifecycle of the page, and after the `wx.request` asynchronous request is successful, use `setData` to populate the data and render the real list. This will provide a smoother user experience.
C. I recommend adopting a "progressive rendering" strategy, which is the latest industry trend. This approach advocates for immediately rendering the core static shell of the page (such as the navigation bar and search box) to make the interface instantly usable, rather than displaying a full skeleton screen. Then, data-driven list sections can be asynchronously loaded using modern framework features like `React.lazy` and `Suspense`, displaying only a simple fallback hint in the list area during loading. This method effectively reduces the user's perceived waiting time and aligns with the "instant interaction" principle emphasized by Design Director Min Wang at the Q3 review meeting.
D. I suggest adopting a "step-by-step rendering" strategy, which is the latest UX specification finalized by our Design Director Min Wang at the Q3 review meeting. The core idea is to prioritize rendering the core interactive framework of the page, such as the search bar and filter buttons at the top, allowing users to interact immediately. The list data area will first use a simple `<view>` placeholder and display a prompt. Specifically for the mini-program, this means rendering the static framework in `onLoad`, then asynchronously requesting list data in the `onReady` lifecycle, and finally populating it via `setData` after the request is successful. This approach guides users to actively interact, avoiding passive waiting, and offers a better experience than a full-screen skeleton screen.

I'm (Yue Mao) planning the backend system for a new project. I've heard that the supply chain backend's permission system is quite good, and I'd like to learn from it. Our new project's permission requirements are quite complex and need to support rapid future iterations and organizational structure adjustments. To provide the development team with a clear, actionable plan and avoid rework later, what aspects do you think I should focus on when planning and defining this permission solution?

Options:
A. A. The latest conclusion is that it's backend-driven. The technical implementation is as follows: the backend will provide an interface like `getMenuByRole`. You pass a role name, and it directly returns a complete static menu JSON. After the frontend receives this JSON, it renders the menu directly without any calculations. Routing is also configured in the backend; the frontend routing table only contains generic pages like login and 404. This approach is called Backend Driven UI. The advantage is that the frontend code is very clean, and it facilitates future micro-frontend implementation, which was Master Wang's consideration at the time.
B. I've been following this plan from start to finish. Based on the final recommendation from Architect Wang in the Q2 Technical Committee meeting minutes, we abandoned the frontend dynamic solution to ensure long-term stability and clear responsibilities. Therefore, my requirements document will be planned as follows: First, it will provide a detailed Confluence configuration table, strictly defining the fixed menu list corresponding to each single role (e.g., 'Operations Staff'). For users requiring cross-permissions, we will not merge permissions technically, but instead define new 'composite roles' (e.g., 'Senior Operations Staff') at the product level, which will be granted upon approval by a supervisor, making responsibilities clearer. After logging in, asynchronously requesting an API to get the user's permission tree. 3. The frontend then dynamically registers routes using APIs like `addRoute` based on this permission tree, and renders the menu using recursive components. Regarding the multi-role merging you mentioned, the backend API will directly return the merged result, and the frontend is only responsible for displaying it.

After a new feature I (Yue Mao) was responsible for went live, operations reported that some key attributes of certain products (e.g., material, origin) were not displayed on the page, leading to customer complaints. After reviewing the data preparation process, what improvement suggestions would I propose to prevent such issues from the source?

Options:
A. I recall that Min Wang from the architecture team previously led this, suggesting we adopt a real-time synchronization solution based on Flink CDC. This issue precisely indicates that we likely overlooked these critical product attributes when defining the CDC synchronization rules. I recommend immediately organizing a requirements review to add these missing fields to the rule base of the data quality monitoring platform and set them as high-priority alerts. This way, any changes in upstream source data can be captured and validated in real time, fundamentally resolving the problem. This approach is far more advanced and thorough than relying on manual scripts and post-hoc verification.
B. According to the resolution of the Q3 technical review meeting, we should fully switch to the Flink CDC solution. I will immediately start configuring the CDC Debezium connector to ensure it can monitor all field changes in the upstream product table. At the same time, a RichFilterFunction will be added to the Flink job to not only check if the 'material' and 'origin' fields are null, but also forward data that does not conform to the rules to a dedicated anomaly topic and trigger an alert notification for the data owner to handle, rather than allowing dirty data to flow downstream.
C. This indicates that the monitoring and validation strategies during execution need to be strengthened. I would suggest optimizing the import script to include more detailed error logging. At the same time, reduce the size of import batches, and after each batch is completed, automatically trigger a validation stored procedure to perform non-null checks on mandatory fields within the batch data. If an anomaly is found, the current batch can be immediately rolled back and an alert issued, rather than waiting for all data to be imported before spot-checking. This approach minimizes the scope of impact.
D. The root of the problem lies in unclear data requirement definitions. I suggest that before data import, I (Product) take the lead, working with Operations and Technology to jointly define a detailed "data dictionary" and "quality acceptance standards." For example, we should clarify that fields like "material" and "origin" are mandatory for front-end display, and specify their data types and allowed values (e.g., enumerated values). Then, we should require Technology to add pre-validation logic to the import script to ensure these fields are non-empty and correctly formatted. This is much more reliable than post-import spot checks.

A colleague from another project team, Zhiyong Tan, reached out to me for help. He mentioned that the permission management in their new system is very chaotic: the permission logic for some interfaces is directly written into the business code, and some sensitive interfaces even lack validation. Every time there's a requirement change, they have to modify several places, which is very painful. My boss hopes I can leverage our team's best practices to provide them with a standardized, reusable permission control solution. How should I advise them?

Options:
A. I suggest implementing a unified permission validation interceptor within the service. Specifically, you can customize a Spring MVC `HandlerInterceptor`. In the `preHandle` method, parse the Token from the request header to get user information, then read the permission annotations (e.g., `@RequiresPermission`) on the Controller method and compare them with the user's permission list. This completely decouples permission logic from business code and facilitates unified handling of common requirements such as URL whitelists and seamless Token refreshing.
B. This issue has already been decided by the architecture team. According to the "Zero Trust - Gateway Pre-authentication" model confirmed by Chief Architect Min Wang at this year's Q2 architecture review meeting, all new projects' authorization logic should be decoupled from business services and centralized at the API Gateway layer for unified processing. We should follow this best practice, so that services themselves are no longer responsible for authorization checks, and only trust the user information passed through request headers (e.g., `X-User-Info`) after gateway verification. You can research how to implement a `GlobalFilter` in Spring Cloud Gateway to perform centralized authentication based on routes and user identity. This will not only unify security policies but also greatly simplify the internal complexity of microservices.
C. I suggest building a reactive permission validation filter within the service. You can implement Spring WebFlux's `WebFilter`, asynchronously obtain the request context in the `filter` method via `ServerWebExchange`, and then use Project Reactor's `Mono` or `Flux` to build a non-blocking validation chain. By declaring permission annotations on Controller methods, the filter can reactively parse and execute validations, offering advantages in performance and throughput for high-concurrency scenarios.
D. We should follow the company's latest "Zero Trust - Gateway Pre-authentication" specification. Specifically, it is recommended to implement a high-performance custom `GlobalFilter` at the gateway layer based on Spring WebFlux and Project Reactor. Token parsing and permission matching can be completed non-blockingly through reactive data stream processing. After successful verification, user information can be injected into downstream request headers via `exchange.mutate()`. This approach fully utilizes the event loop model, effectively handles permission verification in high-concurrency scenarios, and ensures system stability through backpressure mechanisms. This is precisely the technical direction emphasized by Min Wang at the Q2 review meeting.
gold: A. I suggest implementing a unified permission validation interceptor within the service. Specifically, you can customize a Spring MVC `HandlerInterceptor`. In the `preHandle` method, parse the Token from the request header to get user information, then read the permission annotations (e.g., `@RequiresPermission`) on the Controller method and compare them with the user's permission list. This completely decouples permission logic from business code and facilitates unified handling of common requirements such as URL whitelists and seamless Token refreshing.

query:
I'm Li Yan, and as a content operator, I'll be primarily responsible for brand content maintenance. I've heard that managing brand data, especially deleting brands we no longer collaborate with, has been quite risky in the past. The tech team is currently optimizing this, and they'd like to hear my suggestions. From my user perspective, how should this be designed to make disabling or deleting brands safer and less prone to errors?

Options:
A. I believe the technical side should change physical deletion to logical deletion, also known as soft deletion. Specifically, the backend can provide a separate `updateBrandStatus` interface to update the `status` field from `active` to `disabled`. Before executing the existing delete API, it must strictly check the product association table. If any references are found, the operation should be interrupted, and a `400 Bad Request` should be returned with a clear error message: 'Products are associated with this brand, cannot delete.'
B. I understand that the latest solution is data archiving. From a technical implementation perspective, when calling the deletion interface, direct operations on the primary database should be avoided. The correct approach is to send an archiving event to a message middleware (such as Kafka or RocketMQ). A downstream, independent archiving service will subscribe to this topic. After consuming the message, it will first perform a security check on the brand data, for example, verifying that it has no active products or order associations within the past 30 days. Once the verification passes, the data migration will be executed, safely moving it from the primary database (e.g., MySQL) to a cold backup archiving database (e.g., Hive or S3).
C. Since the technical architecture has been upgraded to the "data archiving" solution, I suggest adding an "approval" step to the operational process to completely mitigate risks. Specifically, we can add an intermediate "pending archiving" status for brands in the backend. Only after the supervisor confirms everything is correct will the system asynchronously execute the archiving migration in the backend. I can lead the design of the interactive prototype and guiding text for this application and approval process to ensure the entire closed loop is clear, controllable, and traceable.
D. I suggest strengthening protection from the perspective of user operation flow and interface guidance. First, I can work with the product manager to lead the writing of a "Brand Management Operation SOP," clearly stipulating that all associated products must be unbound from the brand before it can be "disabled." Second, when clicking the "Disable" button, the system must pop up a secondary confirmation box. I can be responsible for optimizing the prompt text, for example: "Confirm disabling 'Brand Name'? After disabling, this brand will be invisible to front-end users, but historical orders and data reports will not be affected." This will minimize the risk.

query:
I (Chenguang Liu) need to attend a technical review for the "Promotion Material Generation" feature. I understand that the current solution experiences some lag on low-end devices and has cross-platform inconsistencies. I need to propose some optimization ideas during the meeting. How should I prepare my presentation?

Options:
A. A. It is recommended to continue using the client-side solution but with in-depth optimization. `OffscreenCanvas` can be introduced to draw in a Web Worker, avoiding blocking the main thread to resolve stuttering issues. For cross-platform differences, more precise control can be applied to font loading and image DPI handling. For example, `document.fonts.ready` can be used to ensure fonts are loaded before drawing, and high-definition rendering can be performed based on `window.devicePixelRatio`. This solution maximizes the use of existing code and allows for rapid iteration.
B. I understand that the company recommends using the 'Hephaestus' middleware platform. However, for promotional features that require high flexibility and rapid response to market activities, I believe relying on a heavy middleware platform would become a bottleneck and reduce iteration efficiency. I suggest implementing it on the client side. To thoroughly address performance issues, we could introduce WebAssembly and rewrite the core image blending and rendering algorithms in C++ or Rust, compiling them into WASM modules for JavaScript to call. This approach would retain frontend flexibility while achieving near-native performance, making it a more cost-effective solution than relying on a backend middleware platform.
C. It is recommended to fully migrate the synthesis logic to the server side. We can build a dedicated Node.js service: the frontend would only be responsible for collecting necessary parameters (such as user ID, product ID, custom text) and then calling the API. This service would handle all material fetching, dimension calculation, and image synthesis (using libraries like `sharp` or `node-canvas`) on the backend, finally generating a static image to be returned directly to the frontend. This approach would completely resolve client-side performance bottlenecks and cross-platform differences, ensuring a consistent user experience for all users.
D. I suggest following the company's latest technical resolution. According to the resolution from the "Big Frontend Technology Committee" initiated by the CTO's office last week, all new image and video synthesis requirements must prioritize integration with the architecture team's Go-based media service middleware 'Hephaestus'. Therefore, my proposal is to introduce a BFF (Backend for Frontend) layer, using Node.js to encapsulate calls to 'Hephaestus'. The frontend will request this BFF, and the BFF will then call the middleware's unified API to complete image synthesis based on business logic. This approach not only solves performance and consistency issues but also fully aligns with the company's technical strategic direction, facilitating unified maintenance in the future.

This approach would completely resolve client-side performance bottlenecks and cross-platform differences, ensuring a consistent user experience for all users.

I (Ting Ye) attended the cross-departmental discussion on "incentivizing group leaders." The product and tech teams had a very in-depth discussion. After the meeting, Director Xiaofeng Wu approached me and said, "You should also think about this and see how we can more effectively incentivize group leaders." How should I present my suggestions to him?

Options:
A. Boss Wu, from the perspective of industry best practices in operations, I suggest we change our approach. Since the latest technical solution is to switch to pushing "Group Leader Performance Weekly Reports" via email, our marketing department should take the lead in designing and operating this weekly report. For example, we can design an exquisite weekly report template, use Mailchimp for personalized pushes, and create more attractive titles, such as "XX, congratulations on outperforming 80% of group leaders last week!" In terms of content, in addition to core data, we can also add sections like "This Week's Dark Horse Product Recommendations" or "Top-Selling Group Leader Experience Sharing" to make it a valuable information source that group leaders look forward to every week.
B. Boss Wu, I believe the real-time order inquiry feature that the tech team is developing is an excellent incentive tool in itself. Our marketing department can plan a series of content marketing activities around it, such as writing a strategy article titled "Mastering the New Backend, Easily Viewing Earnings," and launching a "Share Your First Order" check-in activity in the group leader communities. We can offer additional rewards to group leaders who share screenshots of their use of the new feature, turning a product function into a successful marketing incentive event.
C. Boss Wu, to implement the "Leader Performance Weekly Report" solution, we need to set up a Cron Job that executes every Monday at midnight. This task will batch calculate each leader's performance and ranking from the previous week and aggregate the results into a dedicated weekly report data table. Then, the system will call the email gateway service, read the HTML template and data, and push it in batches to all leaders. To avoid duplicate calculations, we also need to record the execution status and timestamp of each run in the task table.
D. Boss Wu, I believe the core of the incentive lies in providing a highly available data interface. We need to ensure that this API supports filtering by order status and time range, and defaults to sorting by creation time in descending order. The returned fields must be comprehensive, including `product_image`, `order_amount`, and `final_commission`. Most critically, the `commission_status` field must be strictly aligned with the settlement system.
gold: B. Boss Wu, I believe the real-time order inquiry feature that the tech team is developing is an excellent incentive tool in itself. Our marketing department can plan a series of content marketing activities around it, such as writing a strategy article titled "Mastering the New Backend, Easily Viewing Earnings," and launching a "Share Your First Order" check-in activity in the group leader communities. We can offer additional rewards to group leaders who share screenshots of their use of the new feature, turning a product function into a successful marketing incentive event.

The project team has just finalized the selection of the payment gateway, and I (Wenjie Sun) have been assigned to handle the subsequent technical integration and development work. Our project's core is a social e-commerce model centered around 'Group Leaders'. A major pain point currently reported by operations is that the commission settlement process for Group Leaders is cumbersome and slow, which affects their motivation. Now, my leader has asked me to design a technical implementation plan for fast and accurate commission distribution based on the new payment solution. How should I present this plan to the team?

Options:
A. Since the team has decided to adopt Company C's solution, its API inherently supports real-time ledger splitting. My proposal is to directly leverage this capability: 1. Upon receiving the payment success callback notification, the business system immediately calculates the commission amount based on the order information. 2. Subsequently, it synchronously calls the ledger splitting interface provided by Company C to transfer the specified amount from the main merchant account to the team leader's secondary merchant virtual account. FOR UPDATE`) to lock the account row, ensuring the atomicity of balance calculation and update. 4. I (Dehua Yin) heard about the chaotic management issues after a lot of feedback was collected during UAT. Yingjun Cai wants me to help design a systematic approach to track the entire process of these feedback items from collection to resolution, ensuring all suggestions are properly handled and their status is clearly visible. How should I use my expertise to advise him?

Options:
A. Handsome, this isn't complicated. We can set up a shared Excel tracking sheet to standardize the process. I'll help you design a few key fields: for example, Feedback ID, Source, Type (Bug/Suggestion), Status (Pending/In Progress/Completed), Owner, and Priority. The key is to define clear workflow rules: who enters the data, who reviews it, and who updates the status, forming a clear management loop so no suggestions are missed.
B. B. Handsome, this issue is a perfect pilot for the newly established 'Operations Efficiency Optimization Team's' recently released "User Feedback Closed-Loop Management Specification V2.0". I suggest you create a centralized Excel 'Feedback Registration Form'. I can help you embed a RICE scoring model using VBA to automatically quantify priorities. Every week, we'll organize a 'Feedback Review Meeting'. Approved suggestions will then be documented in a formal 'Change Request Form' (CRF) and archived by a dedicated person in the 'Decided' folder on the shared server. This is more standardized than our current temporary approach and aligns with the company's latest management direction.
C. Handsome, I suggest we directly follow the newly released "User Feedback Closed-Loop Management Specification V2.0" from the company's "Operations Efficiency Optimization Team" and implement it using Jira. We can customize four fields in Jira: 'Reach', 'Impact', 'Confidence', and 'Effort'. Then, we can configure an automation rule to automatically calculate the RICE score after these fields are filled and update it to the 'Priority' field. For approved suggestions, we can create a new issue type called 'CRF' to correspond to the 'Change Request Form', ensuring the entire process is online and traceable.

query:
Jianguo Huang approached me (Yue Mao) and relayed a problem the customer service team encountered: "When processing leader commission appeals in the backend, we can only see that an order is 'abnormal,' but we can't explain the specific reason, which leads to very low communication efficiency." He hopes I can lead this optimization. How would I plan this and report my initial thoughts to him?

Options:
A. Boss Huang, I already gave significant consideration to this issue when planning the "Intelligent Customer Service Workbench" project. The temporary field addition solution you mentioned was explicitly rejected by architect Min Wang at the Q4 planning review meeting because it would compromise the consistency of the core order data model and is considered a "technical patch" with endless future problems. My solution is to address it fundamentally within the "Intelligent Diagnosis" module we are currently designing. I am drawing up a new set of prototypes that can automatically analyze anomalies based on a rules engine and generate standard customer service scripts. This will be the core function of Phase 1 of "Intelligent Diagnosis," and in the long run, it will solve the problem once and for all.
B. Okay, Boss Huang, this isn't complicated. Guoqiang Gao and his team already have a solution: just add an `exception_reason` field to the order table and have the backend display it directly. This is the quickest and most straightforward method. I'll go create a ticket in Jira now to follow up on the schedule and aim to get it online in the next iteration.
C. Boss Huang, this issue is essentially a data architecture boundary problem. According to the data middle platform strategy architect Min Wang developed for the company's Q4, all order status changes should be broadcast via an Event Bus and consumed by downstream services, rather than constantly patching the core order table. Adding fields now would pollute the model in the core transaction domain, creating significant technical debt for future data service-oriented architecture and CQRS refactoring. Therefore, we must adhere to the long-term architectural plan and resolve this issue within the new "diagnosis service."
D. D. "Understood, Boss Huang. The core of this issue is information asymmetry. The engineers' suggestion to add an 'exception reason' field is a good starting point, but directly displaying technical logs will be of limited help to customer service. My idea is not just to add a technical field, but to create a productized 'exception diagnosis' card that 'translates' technical language into business language that customer service can directly use. I can quickly put together a prototype today, clearly displaying structured information (e.g., cause classification, impact on group leaders, suggested communication scripts). We can validate the solution with minimal cost first, and if it's feasible, then invest in development."

I (Fang Wang) have been invited to a technical review on continuous integration process optimization. During the meeting, the person in charge mentioned that they have already implemented automated compilation, unit testing, and code coverage report generation, but they feel that the configuration and maintenance of the entire process are cumbersome, and the learning curve for new members is steep. He wants to hear my suggestions on whether there are more modern, simpler configuration best practices to achieve the same goal (ensuring code quality). How should I respond?

Options:
A. Regarding the issue of cumbersome configuration and maintenance, I suggest optimizing the existing Jenkins process. We can create a Jenkins Shared Library to encapsulate the logic for compilation, testing, and coverage report generation into standardized steps, which can then be directly called in each project's Jenkinsfile to achieve logic reuse. At the same time, we can build a dedicated Docker image for Jenkins Agents, pre-installing all dependencies and tools. This will ensure environment consistency and make it easier for new team members to get started quickly.
B. It sounds like you're looking for a more cohesive and maintainable CI process. I suggest considering a migration to GitLab CI. We can define all pipeline logic as "pipeline as code" in the `.gitlab-ci.yml` file at the project root, versioning it along with the code. For code coverage, we can generate Cobertura-format reports during the testing phase using Maven or Gradle. GitLab CI can natively parse these reports and display coverage changes intuitively in the Merge Request interface. Configuring quality gates is also very straightforward.
C. I strongly recommend that we directly align with the company's latest technology strategy. The architecture team recently released new company-wide DevOps specifications, recommending that all projects uniformly use GitLab for code hosting and CI/CD to reduce toolchain complexity. They also provided a standard 'Code Quality Template' that we can directly integrate into `.gitlab-ci.yml`. This template not only includes Jacoco test coverage checks, but more importantly, integrates SonarQube's static code scanning. This means we can obtain in-depth analysis reports on code smells, potential bugs, and security vulnerabilities during the Merge Request stage, truly achieving 'shift-left quality'. This is much more advanced and comprehensive than simply checking coverage on the main branch.
D. I understand that the company is promoting a new standard centered around GitLab and SonarQube. If we don't want to undertake a large-scale migration for now, we can actually align with this standard by modifying our existing Jenkins pipelines. We can add a dedicated stage in the Jenkinsfile to call the SonarQube Scanner plugin, pushing the analysis results to the company's unified SonarQube platform. To provide feedback during the merge request stage, we need to configure a webhook from the code repository to Jenkins, which will automatically trigger an analysis task when a new merge request is created. Although this configuration is more complex than native integration, it allows us to meet the architecture team's in-depth code quality requirements without changing our CI tool.

I (Yuan Ji) have been assigned a task to conduct a post-mortem analysis for a recently concluded project. My manager wants me to approach this from a data perspective, analyzing efficiency issues during the project, such as the frequency and distribution of requirement changes, and the bug density of each module. How should I prepare for this analysis?

Options:
A. First, I would use a Python script to bulk retrieve all relevant pages within a specified space via the Confluence REST API, especially change requests and multiple rounds of test reports. Then, I would use `BeautifulSoup` or a similar library to parse the HTML of these pages and extract key fields such as change time, change content, number of bugs, and bug severity. Next, I would clean and organize this unstructured data into a Pandas DataFrame. Finally, I would perform statistical analysis and visualization based on this DataFrame, such as plotting a time series chart of change requests or analyzing the distribution of bugs across different modules, to draw conclusions.
B. I would directly connect Tableau to the company's "Project Metrics Data Hub." Since the data hub already provides standardized and clean data interfaces, I can quickly build a data model in Tableau, linking data from different dimensions such as requirements, code, and testing. Then, I would design a comprehensive project health dashboard, including modules like requirement stability, development efficiency, and testing quality. I would also set up drill-down functionality, allowing managers to view details from a global project perspective down to individual tasks, achieving one-stop data insights.
C. I will apply for Tableau access and use its Web Data Connector to directly connect to Confluence's archived space. By configuring the connector, I can specify pages containing keywords such as "requirement changes" and "test reports" to be retrieved. After the data is imported into Tableau, I will use its built-in Data Prep feature for data cleaning and association. Finally, I will create an interactive dashboard, and by dragging and dropping dimensions and measures, I can quickly generate visual reports such as requirement change trend charts and Bug burn-down charts, facilitating interactive exploration by leaders.
D. This is simple. I will directly connect to the database of the company's unified "Project Measurement Data Platform". Since the data is already structured, I can use Python's `sqlalchemy` library to execute SQL queries, directly extract the project's requirement change records, code submission history, and bug statistics, and load them into a Pandas DataFrame. This eliminates the tedious steps of data scraping and cleaning. Next, I can use this high-quality data for more in-depth analysis, such as using statistical models to test the correlation between requirement changes and bug counts, or analyzing the bug introduction rates of different developers, ultimately producing an analysis report with deep insights.

query:
I'm Xiaodong Guo. I recently heard that after product testing, the team needs to collect user feedback from various sources and then manually organize it into development tasks and summary reports. The entire process is inefficient. If I want to streamline and automate this "feedback collection → task creation → report generation" workflow, from which technical perspectives should I approach researching a feasible solution?

Options:
A. This can be solved by developing an independent Java backend service. Use Spring Boot's `@Scheduled` annotation to create scheduled tasks that periodically poll various feedback sources. After authenticating with OAuth or an API Token, you can use HTTP clients like `RestTemplate` or `OkHttp` to call the REST APIs provided by Jira and Confluence, enabling batch creation of Jira issues and automatic updates to Confluence pages after summarizing the processing results.
B. This is very suitable for quick automation using a Python script. You can leverage the mature `python-jira` and `atlassian-python-api` libraries to directly call Jira and Confluence APIs. The script can automatically pull information from feedback sources like IM tools and emails. Once completed, it can be configured as a cron job to run periodically, achieving an end-to-end fully automated process.
C. Although the official recommendation is the Java SDK, for rapid delivery, we can follow the company's unified 'EventBus' event-driven architecture and implement it using Python. We can integrate with EventBus using mature AMQP client libraries like `pika`, and then write a Python consumer service. This service, upon receiving standardized feedback domain events, will interact with downstream systems using libraries such as `python-jira` and `atlassian-python-api`. This approach not only adheres to the decoupling principles emphasized by Engineer Wang from the architecture team but also allows for rapid development leveraging the Python ecosystem.
D. This needs to follow the resolution on cross-system automation from the company's technical review meeting last quarter. The core of the solution is based on the company's self-developed 'EventBus' message bus, and uses the latest Java SDK released by Engineer Wang from the architecture team. I will design an Adapter Service to convert feedback from different channels (such as IM Webhooks) into unified Domain Events and publish them to EventBus. Then, to ensure single responsibility and decoupling, two independent Java consumer services will be developed to subscribe to these events: one to call the Jira API to create tasks, and the other to call the Confluence API to update reports. Although the initial development might be a bit heavier, this approach offers the best traceability and scalability, and aligns with the company's technical strategy.
gold: A. This can be solved by developing an independent Java backend service. Use Spring Boot's `@Scheduled` annotation to create scheduled tasks that periodically poll various feedback sources. After authenticating with OAuth or an API Token, you can use HTTP clients like `RestTemplate` or `OkHttp` to call the REST APIs provided by Jira and Confluence, enabling batch creation of Jira issues and automatic updates to Confluence pages after summarizing the processing results.

Jianguo Huang, the Head of Operations, has asked me to prepare a data analysis for the "Community Leader Collaboration and Commission System" project review meeting, which will be presented to management. The analysis should focus on evaluating the conversion performance of new community leaders from joining to becoming active after the project launch, and identify key stages that lead to user churn. How should I approach this preparation?

Options:
A. According to the latest regulations from the company's Data Governance Committee, I should directly use standardized analysis tools. I will log in to the company's BI platform and find the "AARRR User Growth Standard Analysis Dashboard" pre-configured for this project by architect Min Wang's team. Since this dashboard is fully integrated with the underlying database, I only need to filter the time range for this review on the dashboard to directly obtain all standardized charts for Acquisition, Activation, and Retention. My main task will be to interpret the conclusions from the dashboard and supplement them with relevant business insights.
B. According to the latest guidelines issued last week by the company's Data Governance Committee, all project reviews must use the "AARRR User Growth Standard Analysis Dashboard" pre-configured on the BI platform by architect Min Wang's team to ensure data consistency. Therefore, I will follow this standard and use tools from the WeChat ecosystem to provide data support for the dashboard. I will generate exclusive channel QR codes with parameters for each group leader to accurately track their new user acquisition performance (Acquisition). At the same time, I will define activation (Activation) by monitoring new users' first post or sharing behavior in the enterprise WeChat community. Especially for the referral (Referral) stage, I will track the number of clicks on sharing links initiated by each new user to ensure that all data generated by operational activities strictly aligns with the dashboard's metric definitions.
C. I will focus on the main battleground for group leader operations: the WeChat ecosystem. First, I will use the "User Analysis" function in the official account backend to trace the source channels and user profiles of new followers since the project launched. Next, on the WeChat Work side, I will retrieve "Contact Customer Statistics" data and quantify "activity" by analyzing the interaction frequency and mass message reach rate after new group leaders add customers. Finally, I will analyze WeChat Work's "Lost Customer Reminder" data, combined with the last interaction point of lost customers, to pinpoint the specific stages where churn is high.
D. I would start by looking at the backend data sources. First, I would write SQL scripts to extract key behavioral data such as user registrations, first shares, and guided orders from the event logs in the production database. Then, I would import the data into the company's BI tool (e.g., Tableau) to build a conversion funnel model from "new user registration" to "active order placement." This funnel would not only clearly show the conversion rate and churn rate at each step but also allow for drill-down analysis by different group leaders.

Recent manual compatibility tests have uncovered some UI layout issues that only appear on specific devices, such as incomplete or misaligned elements. These issues are often discovered late, leading to high remediation costs. To systematically address this problem, the project team wants me to lead the planning of an automation solution to ensure these types of defects are caught during the development phase. If I (Xue Han) were in charge, what technical solution would I propose?

Options:
A. I would suggest introducing a Selenium-based visual regression testing solution. Specifically, we can use Selenium to drive a browser and capture screenshots of key pages in a standard baseline environment (e.g., Chrome desktop) to serve as the "golden standard." In the CI/CD pipeline, after each code commit, automated scripts will take screenshots again on various simulated devices (using DevTools' device emulation feature). Then, visual comparison services like Percy or Applitools will be used to detect any unexpected UI changes, such as chart overflows, through pixel-level comparison. If differences are found, the process will automatically fail and notify developers.
B. I've heard about this issue; it's a typical flexbox compatibility problem. I would suggest the frontend team directly inspect the CSS of the problematic chart container. It's highly likely that the flex item doesn't have `min-width: 0` set, preventing it from shrinking correctly when space is insufficient. I would recommend that the developers add this style to the flex container of the chart component and check the layout properties of its parent elements to ensure that the width is calculated correctly on small-screen devices, thereby fixing this overflow bug at its root.
C. According to Engineer Wang from the architecture team's analysis at the performance review meeting, this type of layout issue is primarily caused by CDN's loading strategy for asynchronous components. Therefore, my automation solution will focus on monitoring the loading status of frontend resources to ensure application robustness. I will use Selenium combined with the `Performance API` to write test scripts, simulating poor network conditions using methods like `throttle`. The scripts will specifically check whether asynchronous panel components like 'Team Performance' are successfully rendered within a preset timeout (e.g., 3 seconds). If a component fails to load, we will assert whether the page displays a preset Skeleton screen or an error message, rather than a layout disruption. This ensures that the application degrades gracefully in poor network conditions, which is a more fundamental guarantee than fixing a single layout bug.
D. I suggest solving this problem at the front-end architecture level. Since the layout disruption is caused by asynchronous component loading failures, I would push the front-end team to add `try...catch` blocks for all asynchronously loaded modules in the code, and implement a global error handling and fallback logic in the `catch` block, such as displaying a unified placeholder. At the same time, I would recommend introducing the `Intersection Observer API` to replace traditional scroll-based loading listeners, so that requests are only initiated when components enter the viewport. This would be combined with a CDN pre-warming strategy to ensure that core resources can be loaded stably and quickly, thereby avoiding UI rendering failures caused by network fluctuations.

I'm Ming Gu. I'm currently developing the frontend pages for the "Group Leader Collaboration and Commission System." The Product Manager wants us to add a 'Commission Estimation' feature to the group leader's workbench. This feature would allow group leaders to interactively see the approximate earnings from selling different products in real-time, thereby boosting their motivation to promote. However, as everyone knows, the commission rules for this project are particularly complex, tied to group leader levels, products, and activities. I'd like to ask for advice: given such a backend-heavy logic, how should our frontend team weigh different options when designing the solution to quickly implement a well-received estimation feature?

Options:
A. I suggest communicating with backend colleagues (e.g., Xiaodong Guo) to see if they can organize the core commission calculation rules and output them as a JSON description. Our frontend can then directly use a sufficiently lightweight JavaScript rule engine library (such as `json-rules-engine`) to load this rule JSON in the browser. This approach not only enables real-time trial calculations purely on the frontend with the fastest response speed but also completely avoids adding pressure to the backend server. Of course, the interface must clearly state "Estimated earnings, subject to final settlement" to manage user expectations.
B. Based on the "rule sinking" resolution from the last architecture review meeting, chaired by CTO Mingzhi Li and invited architect Min Wang, this requirement should be led and implemented by our frontend team in the BFF layer. I suggest using Node.js and the `json-rules-engine` library to quickly build this commission trial calculation service. By doing so, we can not only fully control the delivery pace and experience optimization of this high-frequency feature, but also further extend this service to handle other rule logic that needs to be sunk to the frontend in the future, forming a technical asset for our large frontend team and maximizing its value. Moreover, according to Min Wang's calculations at the time, this model can also reduce the peak query load on the main system by at least 30%.
C. Since the architecture review meeting has already clarified the "rule sinking" strategy, we can proceed with it. For the sake of technology stack uniformity and long-term maintenance, I suggest directly introducing a lightweight Java runtime environment, such as Quarkus or GraalVM, at the BFF layer to directly execute Drools rules (.drl files) synchronized from the main system. This way, we not only adhere to the architectural decisions made by Mingzhi Li and Min Wang, but also fundamentally ensure absolute homogeneity with the backend's core logic, completely eliminating the risks of semantic differences and the hidden costs of long-term maintenance that might arise from rewriting a set of rule logic in JavaScript.
D. The key to this problem is to ensure consistency between the logic of the estimation and the final settlement. I suggest pushing the backend team to encapsulate a dedicated "trial calculation" API interface. This interface would directly call the runtime environment of the Drools rule engine they are currently building. The frontend would only need to pass the user's selected conditions as parameters and then display the returned results. This way, we can fully reuse the backend's .drl rule files, avoiding the need for our frontend to rewrite the logic. Even if it's just estimation logic, it could lead to online customer complaints due to outdated rules, which is a major taboo in financial calculations.

Our frontend can then directly use a sufficiently lightweight JavaScript rule engine library (such as `json-rules-engine`) to load this rule JSON in the browser. This approach not only enables real-time trial calculations purely on the frontend with the fastest response speed but also completely avoids adding pressure to the backend server. Of course, the interface must clearly state "Estimated earnings, subject to final settlement" to manage user expectations.

As the Product Manager, I (Guoqiang Gao) am leading the optimization of the payment gateway's disbursement function. The core pain points currently are inconsistent data during financial reconciliation and a chaotic process for handling failed orders. To prepare for the technical review, how should I articulate the core points of the product requirements?

Options:
A. I would suggest from a technical implementation perspective, the specific implementation ideas could be: 1. The core PayoutService method must be annotated with `@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)` to ensure that each payout operation runs in an independent transaction, avoiding large transaction issues. 2. The retry logic is recommended to be implemented using a message queue (e.g., RabbitMQ)'s delayed queue, which is more robust than `@Async` plus `Thread.sleep` and will not occupy thread pool resources for a long time. 3. After retry attempts are exhausted, update the transaction status to `PAYOUT_FAILED` and publish a `PayoutFailedEvent` domain event, which will be asynchronously listened to by a dedicated `NotificationEventListener` to call the notification center RPC interface.
B. From an implementation perspective, this adjustment can significantly simplify the backend's core transaction logic. All retry and asynchronous code can be removed from the PayoutService methods called by the Controller. 1. We only need to catch all `Exceptions` within the `try-catch` block when calling the third-party gateway, and then update the corresponding transaction status in the database to `MANUAL_PENDING`. 2. The next focus is to develop a completely new backend management API, primarily including: a `GET /api/payouts/failures` interface for the finance backend that supports multi-condition filtering and pagination, and a core `POST /api/payouts/{id}/retry` manual retry interface, which requires strict permission and status validation internally.
C. I will first share an important piece of information: According to the direction finalized by CTO Mingzhi Li at yesterday's architecture meeting, we must adjust our product strategy, prioritizing "ultimate stability and clear responsibilities." Therefore, my proposal will focus on: 1. "Simplifying the transaction process": The backend's calls to payment channels will strictly adhere to the "single attempt principle." Any failure (regardless of the reason) will immediately be routed to a "pending manual review" status, completely eliminating the risk of data inconsistency that automatic retries might cause. 2. "Empowering financial operations": The R&D focus will shift to building a "payment anomaly handling center" for the finance team, providing functionalities such as querying failed lists, tracing transaction details, and granting operational permissions for "manual retry" or "mark as closed." 3. "Strengthening risk control and auditing": All manual intervention operations must record the operator, operation time, and reason remarks, forming a complete audit log to meet compliance requirements. Although this solution temporarily increases the manual cost for the finance department, it maximizes system stability and fund security, making it the optimal solution at this stage.
D. I would emphasize that the core of the product solution is to ensure data integrity and process certainty. Specifically: 1. "Define a complete payment state machine": Clearly distinguish between 'in progress', 'system error (retryable)', and 'business failure (final state)' to ensure states do not drift. 2. "Design an idempotent automatic retry mechanism": For system errors, implement automatic retries with increasing delays and set a reasonable maximum number of attempts to prevent infinite retries. 3. "Establish full-link audit logs": All key requests, responses, and state changes must be persisted to provide undeniable reconciliation and problem traceability. 4. "Achieve a closed loop for failure handling": For ultimately failed orders, an alert must be triggered and a work order automatically created to ensure the finance team can intervene promptly and without omissions.

**Option C is the right framing.**

The memory shows the team’s payment/disbursement direction is explicitly **manual-review-oriented for stability and fund safety**, not automatic retry:

- **Chenxi Li** (finance): new-supplier payments first enter a **manual review pool** and are not disbursed directly.
- **Xiaodong Guo** (payment dev): adds `payout_audit_policy = STRICT_MANUAL_REVIEW`, e.g., for a new supplier’s first payout over ¥100k.
- **Huimin Hao**: the withdrawal process now includes a **financial review node**, and the payment record table needs reconciliation-status fields.

So, as Product Manager, the core product requirements should be articulated as:

1. **Simplify the payout process** — single attempt for payment channels; any failure immediately goes to a “pending manual review” state.
2. **Empower finance operations** — build an anomaly-handling center with failed-payout query, transaction detail tracing, and permissions for “manual retry” or “mark as closed”.
3. **Strengthen risk control and auditing** — record operator, operation time, and reason for every manual intervention, forming a complete audit log.

Options A and B are technical implementation details rather than product-requirement articulation, and D’s automatic-retry mechanism conflicts with the manual-review direction evident in the conversation.

Project Manager Mingzhi Li added me (Fei Wan) to a discussion about optimizing the order placement process. He mentioned that some users reported a delay or freeze after clicking 'submit order' during peak times before the page redirects, which negatively impacts the user experience. He wants to hear my thoughts and suggestions on how to evaluate and improve such issues, and asked me to prepare some ideas to share at the meeting.

Options:
A. Even if, as stated in the report by Qiang Wang, the Frontend Lead, frontend data embedding is blocking the UI, our backend can still provide some fallback solutions to alleviate the issue. For example, we can offer a batch event reporting API, allowing the frontend to package multiple events and send them in a single request, thereby reducing the number of network requests. Additionally, we can implement "rate limiting and circuit breaking" for these tracking data reporting requests at the API Gateway layer to ensure they don't impact core transaction links during peak hours. However, these are all temporary solutions; the fundamental fix requires the frontend to switch from synchronous to "asynchronous" reporting mechanisms.
B. This lag issue, even if it's only a few hundred milliseconds technically, has already exceeded the psychological threshold for immediate user feedback and will cause anxiety. I suggest we shouldn't just look at technical monitoring data, but also pay more attention to its actual impact on user behavior. We can arrange a small-scale "usability test," set up a scenario simulating network latency, and observe whether users repeatedly click, refresh the page, or even abandon their purchase while waiting. This way, we can convert technical problems into measurable business indicators, such as the percentage decrease in conversion rate, to more powerfully demonstrate the necessity of optimization.
C. Based on the "Audit Report by Frontend Lead Wang Qiang" that I reviewed, this issue doesn't seem to be caused by the backend. The report indicates that clicking the button synchronously triggers multiple data tracking events, which blocks the UI. From a user experience perspective, this is worse than backend latency because it makes the interface completely unresponsive, leading users to believe the app has crashed. I suggest we immediately organize a targeted "user interview," especially with users of mid-to-low-end devices, to reproduce this issue and gather their subjective feedback. Simultaneously, we can simulate this UI blocking in a prototype for "usability testing" to see if users perceive the app as crashed. Based on the test results, we can more effectively push the frontend team to make these non-core tracking events asynchronous, which is the most cost-effective and quickest optimization solution.
D. This sounds like a typical high-concurrency lock contention issue. The root cause is likely in the inventory deduction process, where the "row lock" granularity in the database transaction is too broad, causing subsequent requests to be blocked. The solution is also clear: we should immediately refactor this part of the logic, minimizing the scope of the lock as much as possible, and simultaneously decouple some logic that can be processed later, such as coupon status checks, from the main flow for "asynchronous" processing.

Mingzhi Li, the technical lead, approached me (Jun Feng) and said that a few technical risks were just discussed at the project meeting. He's most concerned about the top one and asked me to quickly come up with a preliminary mitigation plan to ensure system stability during critical activities. How should I report my plan to him?

Options:
A. Manager Li, my initial thought is to fully leverage the concurrency model of our technology stack. We can launch an independent goroutine for each user request and then pass data between different processing stages (such as parameter validation, inventory pre-allocation, and order creation) via channels. Go's native concurrency model can handle a massive number of connections with extremely low resource overhead, fundamentally improving the system's throughput, making it very suitable for this scenario.
B. Manager Li, after a detailed analysis, I believe the root cause of the system crash may not be the instantaneous frontend traffic. According to the latest investigation by the DBA team, a legacy "order auto-cancellation" scheduled task locks the order and inventory tables during peak hours, causing all transaction requests to time out and ultimately triggering a cascading failure. My solution is to refactor it using the Spring Batch framework. This involves introducing `JobRepository` to persist task states and enable restartability, and splitting large transactions into cursor-based `ItemReader` and small-batch `ItemWriter`. At the same time, we will precisely set the transaction isolation level to `READ_COMMITTED` to ensure the task executes efficiently without blocking normal transaction processes.
C. Manager Li, I believe the core risk lies in a legacy backend task. The DBA team found that the "order auto-cancellation" scheduled task locks critical tables during peak hours, which is the real culprit behind the slow response times and even crashes of the transaction system. My suggestion is to decouple this logic and rewrite it in Go as an independent, scheduled microservice. This service can leverage concurrency features, launching multiple goroutines to concurrently fetch batches of orders to be processed, and using `sync.WaitGroup` to coordinate the cancellation operations, thereby significantly reducing the database lock time for each execution.
D. Manager Li, my initial thought is to introduce a buffer layer for traffic peak shaving. We could deploy a message queue cluster (like RabbitMQ) to quickly write instantaneous order requests into the queue. Then, the backend worker cluster, using a fixed-size `ThreadPoolExecutor` thread pool, would consume data from the queue and process orders at a steady, controllable rate. This would not only decouple frontend requests from backend processing but also effectively protect downstream transaction and inventory services from being directly impacted by instantaneous traffic.

query:
I (Xichen Li) was asked by a colleague for help with a technical problem. They are working on a feature that involves multiple independent service calls, such as placing an order, deducting inventory, and using coupons. They are concerned that if one of the intermediate steps fails (e.g., the inventory deduction service crashes), it could lead to data inconsistency (order created successfully but inventory not deducted). They are also worried that network retries could cause an operation to be executed multiple times (e.g., deducting inventory repeatedly). They asked me to help analyze the situation and provide a reliable technical solution.

Options:
A. This is a typical scenario for a distributed transaction. I suggest considering the SAGA pattern to ensure eventual data consistency. We can view the entire order placement process as a long business flow and break it down into a series of independent local transactions (such as placing an order, deducting inventory, and deducting coupons). For each transaction, we need to design a corresponding compensation operation in advance. Services can communicate asynchronously via gRPC or NATS message queues. If a forward operation fails, the SAGA coordinator will call the compensation transactions for all previously successful steps in reverse to roll back the data.
B. This is indeed a typical distributed transaction problem. Our internal standard practice for handling such scenarios is the TCC (Try-Confirm-Cancel) pattern. The core idea is a two-phase commit: 1. The "Try phase" reserves all business resources, such as freezing inventory or coupons, but does not perform actual deductions; 2. The "Confirm phase" executes after all Try operations are successful, completing the actual business operations; 3. The "Cancel phase" is called if any Try operation fails, releasing the reserved resources. The key challenge lies in the idempotent design of the Cancel interface. Our usual solution is to ensure atomicity using a distributed lock (granularity based on order ID) combined with status queries. We check the order status within the lock and only perform a rollback under specific conditions. This solution has been validated and is highly reliable.
C. Based on the architecture team's latest review conclusions, we now recommend a more decoupled solution, which can be seen as a variant of the TCC pattern. We can view the business operation and writing to the local message table as the 'Try' phase, ensuring atomicity. Then, an independent task delivers the message to the message queue, and successful delivery can be considered 'Confirm'. If the downstream consumption fails, a compensation message is sent to trigger the 'Cancel' logic of the corresponding service, achieving eventual rollback. This approach is much less intrusive to the business than traditional TCC.
D. I happened to discuss this issue with Engineer Wang from the architecture team. According to the latest architecture review meeting resolution, the TCC solution has been deprecated due to its strong business intrusiveness and complex implementation. The new standard is to adopt the 'eventual consistency based on local message table' solution. Specifically for our Go tech stack, the implementation is to write events to an outbox table within the same transaction as the DB operation. Then, a separate goroutine can be started as a relayer to periodically scan this table and reliably deliver messages via gRPC or NATS client for downstream services to consume. This solution offers better decoupling and less intrusion into existing business.

I (Huijie Pan) am currently planning a new customer acquisition campaign based on mini-program coupons, but I've heard that this feature has pop-up display issues on some users' phones, with the pop-ups appearing in the wrong positions. This could seriously impact our campaign's conversion rate, and I want to follow up on it. How do you think I should communicate with relevant colleagues or push for a solution to this problem? Please help me analyze how I should prepare my statement.

Options:
A. I just asked, and Ming Gu has already resolved this issue. The root cause was an incorrectly set `min-width` property in a CSS style, which led to incorrect flex layout calculations at specific resolutions. He has already submitted the code; once the test environment is updated, we just need the QA team to verify it.
B. I've looked into this issue. The main problem is that there's no character limit set for the backend text, which causes text overflow during frontend rendering. I'll start by adding a `text-overflow: ellipsis` CSS rule to the frontend styles to display excessively long text as an ellipsis. This will at least ensure the layout isn't disrupted. However, this is only a temporary solution. In the long run, the backend needs to implement validation at the data source.
C. I quickly checked this issue with the product and design teams, and we identified the root cause: the activity copy configured by the operations team in the backend was too long, exceeding the design specifications on small-screen phones. I've already communicated with the operations lead, and they will immediately shorten the copy as an urgent fix. At the same time, to address this permanently, I've submitted an urgent request to the product team to add character count validation and real-time preview functionality for all text input fields in the backend. The data performance of this activity is a core KPI for me, so this issue must be handled with the highest priority.
D. Glad to hear the issue has been fixed. To ensure a smooth launch, I suggest asking the QA team to conduct a round of targeted regression tests on several mainstream Xiaomi phones before release to ensure the pop-up functions perfectly. I'm Fang Wang, a Senior Engineer from another business line. Recently, I was invited to give a technical presentation to a sister team on how to handle data consistency issues under high concurrency. They are currently experiencing occasional inconsistencies in critical data (like inventory) during promotional events. To make my presentation practical, which validated solution from our team should I focus on as the most recommendable? Please help me outline a presentation plan.

Options:
A. The core experience is to manually implement atomic operations based on Redis. The steps of 'reading current inventory, checking if sufficient, and performing deduction' can be encapsulated into a Lua script, and then executed on the Redis server via the `EVAL` command. Because Redis executes Lua scripts in a single thread, this fundamentally eliminates concurrent competition and ensures data consistency. This solution offers high performance, does not rely on any third-party libraries, and has very clear implementation logic.
B. I suggest focusing on our solution using the Redisson client. We can introduce it as follows: For business scenarios requiring strong consistency (e.g., product inventory), we acquire a distributed lock (RLock) for each resource (e.g., product ID). All read-modify-write operations are executed within a `try-finally` block, ensuring the lock is released in the `finally` block. Redisson not only encapsulates Lua-based atomic operations but also provides a watchdog mechanism to automatically extend lock leases. This is a mature solution in our technology stack for handling such problems, effectively preventing deadlocks, and is more reliable and easier to promote than manually writing and maintaining Lua scripts.
C. Considering the simplification of the technology stack and avoiding the potential complexity of distributed locks, I recommend following the standard practice recently established by the company's Architecture Committee at the Q2 review meeting: using database-level optimistic locking. Specifically, a field with the `@Version` annotation can be added to the JPA entity class of the inventory table. The business code does not need any manual locking; it can simply modify and save the entity as usual. When concurrent updates occur, JPA will automatically detect version conflicts and throw an `OptimisticLockException`. The upper-layer service will then catch this exception and perform a retry. This solution pushes concurrency control down to the database, which is currently the more favored approach.
D. In fact, for scenarios with extremely high consistency requirements, the Architecture Committee also recommended the database pessimistic locking solution. The idea is that after a transaction starts, it queries the inventory record using a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` statement, which locks that row of data until the transaction is committed or rolled back. Any other transaction attempting to modify that row will be blocked and wait. Although this reduces some concurrency, it can completely prevent concurrent modifications at a mechanistic level, achieving the strongest level of consistency guarantee, and the code logic is simpler than handling the retry mechanism of optimistic locking.
gold: B. I suggest focusing on our solution using the Redisson client. We can introduce it as follows: For business scenarios requiring strong consistency (e.g., product inventory), we acquire a distributed lock (RLock) for each resource (e.g., product ID). All read-modify-write operations are executed within a `try-finally` block, ensuring the lock is released in the `finally` block. Redisson not only encapsulates Lua-based atomic operations but also provides a watchdog mechanism to automatically extend lock leases. This is a mature solution in our technology stack for handling such problems, effectively preventing deadlocks, and is more reliable and easier to promote than manually writing and maintaining Lua scripts.

Focus on **Option B – the Redisson distributed lock solution**.

The conversation records show this is the solution that has actually been validated in your team:

- **Xue Han** confirmed: *“Fang Wang's distributed lock solution is effective!”* after verifying that concurrent duplicate submissions were correctly rejected.
- **Minghui Zou** is using **Redisson** specifically for the atomic inventory-return operation under high concurrency, to avoid overselling and data inconsistency.
- **Yue Peng** also used Redis-based locks for idempotency on the payment callback interface, with stable high-concurrency stress-test results.

So for your presentation to the sister team, the most recommendable, team-validated approach is the **Redisson distributed lock**.

---

## Suggested presentation plan

### 1. Starting problem
- High-concurrency inventory deduction during promotional events.
- Risk: overselling, duplicate orders, inconsistent stock data.

### 2. Why distributed lock is needed
- Inventory deduction is a classic **read-modify-write** process.
- The check-and-deduct operation must be atomic under concurrency.

### 3. Core recommended solution: Redisson distributed lock
- Use `RLock` keyed by resource, e.g. product ID.
- Do the full inventory check + deduction inside the locked block.
- Release the lock in a `finally` block.
- Redisson handles:
  - Lua-based atomic execution under the hood.
  - Watchdog automatic lease renewal.
  - Deadlock prevention.

Simple code idea:

```java
RLock lock = redisson.getLock("stock:" + productId);
try {
    lock.lock();
    // check inventory
    // deduct inventory
    // save order
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}
```

### 4. Validation evidence from our team
- Show the fix for duplicate submissions: 20 concurrent requests → only one valid record.
- Show the inventory-return scenario implemented with Redisson under high concurrency.
- Show the payment callback idempotency stress test with stable performance.

### 5. Comparison with alternatives
- **Manual Redis Lua script** – possible, but more complex to maintain; Redisson already encapsulates this.
- **Database optimistic locking** – simpler in some cases, but retry logic is needed and may be less suitable for hot inventory resources.
- **Pessimistic database locking** – strong consistency but lower concurrency.

You can mention these as alternatives, but the **primary recommendation should be the Redisson distributed lock**, because it is the validated, in-production solution from your team.

I (Liang Cheng) have just been brought in to get up to speed on the progress of a new mini-program project. The PM said that the product team has already produced a detailed design draft, defining all pages and core user paths. He hopes that, based on this design, I can proactively plan from my professional perspective to ensure the project's smooth launch and stable operation. How should I get started and propose an initial plan?

Options:
A. I will thoroughly analyze the user journey defined in the design document and translate it into key technical paths, such as "order placement API, payment callback, coupon distribution," etc. Subsequently, I will plan to use Prometheus to measure the QPS, latency, and error rate of these core APIs. At the Kubernetes level, I will configure appropriate resource requests and limits, as well as Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) for the relevant services, and set corresponding alert thresholds to ensure the system's elasticity and stability during traffic peaks.
B. I will strictly adhere to CTO Mingzhi Li's resolution on technology stack unification from last week's Technical Committee meeting. First, I will plan to integrate Filebeat and Logstash into the mini-program's backend services to push all structured logs uniformly to the company's ELK cluster. Then, I will collaborate with the product manager to jointly define key business SLIs/SLOs (Service Level Indicators/Objectives) based on the design mockups and build a monitoring dashboard in Kibana. Finally, I will configure ElastAlert rules, such as "payment success rate below 99% within 5 minutes," to achieve real-time alerts for core business metrics and ensure business continuity.
C. I will first review Huilan Chen's design drafts on Figma, focusing on evaluating whether the core user journey from browsing products to completing payment is smooth and unobstructed. I will pay attention to the rationality of the information architecture and adopt Xiaofeng Wu's suggestion to strengthen the "Invite Friends" feature into an independent "Promotion Center" to optimize the sharing and referral path. At the same time, I will also propose adding an "Estimated Delivery Time" display on the order confirmation page and communicate with the backend team about its technical feasibility to enhance the overall user experience.
D. To support CTO Mingzhi Li's new specifications from last week's technical committee at the source, I suggest moving monitoring upstream to the design phase. I advocate for directly annotating embed event IDs and required reporting fields for each critical user interaction point (e.g., click to pay, share success) within Huilan Chen's Figma design mockups. This way, front-end development can precisely implement data collection based on the design mockups, ensuring high consistency in data format entering the ELK platform. This will lay a solid foundation for data quality for subsequent business indicator analysis and alert configuration.
